title: The MICrONS in-degree link to calcium timescale (rho 0.16) repeats but follows the trace signal fraction; after controls, more inputs do not give longer timescales in 12,726 mouse neurons
abstract:
Question: Zenari et al. (2026) report that MICrONS neurons with a higher in-degree have a wider autocorrelation of the raw calcium trace at rest (Spearman rho about 0.16, no controls). They use this as support for a theory in which in-degree sets intrinsic timescales. Does the relation stay after controls?

Approach: we extracted the fluorescence traces of 12,726 functionally matched excitatory neurons in 13 MICrONS scans (DANDI:000402). We measured the half-width at half-maximum (HWHM) of the autocorrelation in the monitor-off epoch and a noise-robust decay time (autocorrelation normalized at lag 1). In-degree came from the v1300 connection graph. The plan was fixed before any timescale was computed.

Results: the published correlation repeats (rho 0.163 in 890 dendrite-proofread neurons). But the HWHM follows the lag-1 autocorrelation, which is the signal fraction of the trace (Spearman 0.96); half of the neurons have an HWHM below one frame. In every scan, in-degree correlates with HWHM as much as with the signal fraction. With controls for signal fraction, the in-degree slope on log HWHM fell from +0.16 to -0.01 (95% CI -0.035 to 0.016). With controls that do not use the autocorrelation (brightness, reliability, sparseness, cell type, area, position, nucleus size), it was +0.001 (-0.021 to 0.023). The noise-robust decay time (median 2.2 s) had no raw link to in-degree and a small negative slope after controls (-0.10, -0.135 to -0.073), and no clear slope after control for total input synapses. Excitatory and inhibitory in-degree, synapse counts, and timescales of repeated-movie residuals gave no positive link either.

Conclusion: in this calcium dataset, the in-degree/timescale correlation comes from trace signal fraction, cell type and position, not from longer timescales of neurons with more inputs. Limitations: one mouse; calcium (GCaMP6s) not spikes; the noise-robust time has moderate split-half reliability (0.35); our presynaptic set is a proxy for the proofread set.

display.caption: Fig. 1. The HWHM of the calcium autocorrelation follows the signal fraction of the trace. (a) Model autocorrelation with a fixed true decay time (1, 2 or 4 s) and white imaging noise: the HWHM changes about tenfold when only the noise changes. (b) Observed HWHM against the lag-1 autocorrelation in the monitor-off epoch, 12,726 neurons (two lower bands: two frame rates). (c) Per scan (marker size = neurons), the in-degree correlation with HWHM (blue) equals the in-degree correlation with the lag-1 autocorrelation; the noise-robust decay time (orange) does not follow it.

Fig. 2. Standardized slope of log timescale on log in-degree (extended-axon presynaptic neurons) as controls are added from left to right. Blue: log HWHM (published measure). Orange: log noise-robust decay time. (a) 890 neurons with proofread dendrites; (b) all 12,726 excitatory neurons. Bars: 95% CI clustered by scan. The positive HWHM slope goes to zero when the lag-1 autocorrelation is controlled.

Fig. 3. Full-model slopes (all pre-set controls, 95% CI clustered by scan) for seven wiring predictors and four timescale measures. No wiring measure gives the positive slope that the degree theory predicts.
